source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 3, pp. 141–154; user-supplied Chapter 3 continuation (Nov. 24, 2026)

coverage.syllabus: Lubbers Fall 2026: § 3.4 Administrative Judges and Decisional Independence, pp. 141–154
coverage.notes: Uses actual casebook text; separately assigned Canvas materials (Cox, Lubbers articles, EO 13,843) not assumed furnished

topics.title: § 3.4 / § 3.4.1 — Administrative Judges and Decisional Independence (pp. 141–148)
topics.description: Assigned reading: Type A/B/C taxonomy, ALJ selection, tenure and agency policy, ACUS Recommendation 92–7, current doctrinal questions as presented in book.

entries.title: Type A adjudication: APA on-the-record hearing, ALJ default
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 3, pp. 141–154; user-supplied Chapter 3 continuation (Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: Type A hearing is covered by APA §§ 554, 556, 557 and ordinarily presided over by ALJ with specific statutory tenure, pay and separation safeguards.
entries.laymanExplanation: A full federal APA trial-style hearing normally uses the protected administrative law judge.
entries.legalExplanation: Exception if organic statute specifies otherwise. Textbook reports bulk of ~1,900 federal ALJs at SSA at time of publication.
entries.examApplication: Start by checking APA § 554(a) gateway; do not assume every evidentiary hearing is Type A.
entries.examTrap: More formal procedure alone does not prove Type A statutory classification.

entries.title: Type B: evidentiary hearing not governed by APA Type A gateway
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 3, pp. 141–154; user-supplied Chapter 3 continuation (Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: Type B hearings are required by statute, regulations or executive order but do not meet Type A gateway; ordinarily presided over by agency administrative judge (AJ), not protected federal ALJ.
entries.laymanExplanation: A hearing can be very trial-like and still not qualify under APA's formal hearing statute.
entries.legalExplanation: Important Type B examples include EOIR immigration proceedings, veterans benefits, Environmental Appeals Board; regulations often supply record exclusivity, ex parte controls, written reasons and appeal protections.
entries.examApplication: Differentiate statute-mandated procedures and APA independent ALJ guarantees.
entries.examTrap: The text emphatically says Type B should not simply be called 'informal adjudication'.

entries.title: Type C: non-evidentiary informal adjudication
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 3, pp. 141–154; user-supplied Chapter 3 continuation (Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: Type C means adjudications not involving trial-type evidentiary hearings; process varies widely, and modern ACUS best practices address flexible notice, presentation, reasons, internal review, advocacy and conflict avoidance.
entries.laymanExplanation: The usual less-formal agency decision, like many benefits or licensing applications.
entries.legalExplanation: ACUS Rec. 2023–5 encourages tailored notice, representation by lawyer/lay advocate, statement of reasons, impartiality protections and ombuds access; recommendations not binding.
entries.examApplication: Classify case first before applying procedure requirements; assess due process separately.
entries.examTrap: Don't assume every Type C case has no procedural safeguards.

entries.title: ALJs versus AJs: structural independence
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 3, pp. 141–154; user-supplied Chapter 3 continuation (Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: Federal Type A ALJs have statutory protections on selection, salary, discipline and function; Type B AJs vary and normally lack same guaranteed protections.
entries.laymanExplanation: Two people can both preside over hearings, but only some have strong federal job protections.
entries.legalExplanation: ACUS Rec. 92–7 worried move to AJs may reduce national adjudicative uniformity and perceived impartiality.
entries.examApplication: Identify title, governing law and independence features instead of just name tag.
entries.examTrap: Being an AJ does not mean unfair hearing; independent protections may be agency-specific.

entries.title: ACUS Recommendation 2016–4 for Type B hearings
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 3, pp. 141–154; user-supplied Chapter 3 continuation (Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: Best practices for Type B mirror much of Type A: exclusive record, ex parte restrictions, separate prosecution/adjudication, written findings, agency head appeals, rights to rebut and more.
entries.laymanExplanation: Even if federal APA isn't mandatory, an agency can adopt fairness protections in its own rules.
entries.legalExplanation: ACUS also recommends representation, discovery, openness, remote hearing tools and precedential decisions; guidance only.

entries.title: ACUS Recommendation 92–7 — independent but accountable ALJ
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 3, pp. 141–154; user-supplied Chapter 3 continuation (Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: ACUS explained administrative judiciary legitimacy as combination of impartial factfinders, agency head policy supervision, consistency and speed; proposed broader ALJ use and appraisals for productivity and behavior.
entries.laymanExplanation: Let the hearing judge be neutral but keep agency heads in control of regulatory policy and avoid endlessly slow dockets.
entries.legalExplanation: The cited Recommendation 92–7 was never implemented; book notes ALJ opposition and ACUS's defunding/revival history. Do not treat its suggested performance standards as law.
entries.examApplication: Use as competing policy proposal, not enacted statutory duties.

entries.title: ALJ discipline and removal: good cause; MSPB hearing
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 3, pp. 141–154; user-supplied Chapter 3 continuation (Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: Traditional federal ALJ removal/discipline requires good cause established before Merit Systems Protection Board; casebook describes ALJs as outside ordinary performance-appraisal regime.
entries.laymanExplanation: Agency boss cannot fire ALJ just for an unpopular decision; discipline for genuine neglect of duties can be appropriate.
entries.legalExplanation: ACUS's 92–7 proposed systematic performance evaluation but never implemented; Abrams and Shapiro demonstrate good cause in documented persistent unproductivity.
entries.examApplication: Distinguish poor performance/backlog misconduct from political retaliation for substantive adjudication.
entries.examTrap: Do not say ALJs completely immune from discipline.

entries.title: Appointments Clause: ALJs are inferior officers; Lucia
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 3, pp. 141–154; user-supplied Chapter 3 continuation (Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: ALJs exercising significant statutory authority are inferior officers and must be appointed by President, court of law or department head; SEC staff appointment failed.
entries.laymanExplanation: ALJ is an officer; merely having agency staff hire that officer can violate Constitution.
entries.legalExplanation: Lucia v SEC led to new hearing before properly appointed adjudicator and affects executive-branch ALJ appointment practices.
entries.examApplication: Ask who actually appointed ALJ and whether office qualifies under Article II.
entries.examTrap: Do not confuse lawful appointment with tenure protection and due-process neutrality.

entries.title: Lucia v. SEC, 585 U.S. 237 (2018) — ALJ appointment
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 3, pp. 141–154; user-supplied Chapter 3 continuation (Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: SEC's ALJs were appointed by agency staff, not commission head; violates Appointments Clause for inferior officers.
entries.laymanExplanation: ALJ job is important enough to require constitutionally proper appointment.
entries.legalExplanation: Opinion itself not reproduced; textbook supplies result and cross-reference.
entries.examApplication: Apply appointment remedy distinct from bias.
entries.sourceRole: Case discussed only in assigned casebook Notes; full opinion not reproduced

entries.title: ALJ tenure in independent agencies — unresolved constitutional issue in book
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 3, pp. 141–154; user-supplied Chapter 3 continuation (Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: Double-layer good-cause protections for SEC ALJs plus independent agency heads raised Article II removal challenge; circuits split in cited cases; Supreme Court Jarkesy decision resolved Seventh Amendment issue without deciding removal.
entries.laymanExplanation: There was an open legal fight over whether President has enough control when ALJ and commissioners both insulated.
entries.legalExplanation: Fifth Circuit Jarkesy held protections invalid, Supreme Court didn't reach it; Leachco (10th) and Decker Coal (9th) upheld. Source describes unresolved controversy as of publication.
entries.examApplication: In exam state jurisdiction and distinguish binding Supreme Court holding from lower-court split; note independent head vs executive agency.
entries.examTrap: Do not say SEC v Jarkesy (2024) itself struck down ALJ good-cause tenure.

entries.title: SEC v. Jarkesy, 603 U.S. 109 (2024) — limited holding noted
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 3, pp. 141–154; user-supplied Chapter 3 continuation (Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: Supreme Court decided jury-trial requirement in SEC penalty proceeding, declined to resolve ALJ double-for-cause removal question.
entries.laymanExplanation: The Supreme Court won’t necessarily answer every issue raised in an appeal.
entries.legalExplanation: Source notes constitutional status of ALJs as continuing dispute; don't add unprovided 2026 developments.
entries.examApplication: Contrast appointments under Lucia and Seventh Amendment under Jarkesy.
entries.sourceRole: Case discussed only in assigned casebook Notes; full opinion not reproduced

entries.title: Executive Order 13843 and EO 14029 — ALJ hiring change
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 3, pp. 141–154; user-supplied Chapter 3 continuation (Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: 2018 presidential order removed ALJ positions from competitive civil service rating/exam requirements, allowing agency heads more discretion; textbook says Biden-era order largely adhered to process.
entries.laymanExplanation: Agency heads got wider latitude to pick ALJs, which could improve expertise or invite political selection.
entries.legalExplanation: Original OPM competitive ranking was slow and paid little attention to subject expertise; ACUS Rec. 2019–2 urged published objective criteria and neutral hiring panels.
entries.examApplication: Discuss tradeoff: speed/expertise versus actual or perceived impartiality.

entries.title: ACUS Recommendation 2019–2 — neutral hiring safeguards
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 3, pp. 141–154; user-supplied Chapter 3 continuation (Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: ACUS urged agencies to publish qualifications, screen applicants, and protect actual and apparent impartiality after broader appointment discretion.
entries.laymanExplanation: Giving bosses choice should go with transparent hiring rules.
entries.legalExplanation: The recommendation is policy guidance, not mandatory federal regulation.

entries.title: Ass'n of Administrative Law Judges v. Colvin, 777 F.3d 402 (7th Cir. 2015)
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 3, pp. 141–154; user-supplied Chapter 3 continuation (Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: SSA case goal of 500–700 annual decisions did not itself violate ALJ independence, even if arguable quota.
entries.laymanExplanation: A workload goal isn't automatically pressure to decide for agency.
entries.legalExplanation: Court rejected union's argument faster case targets forced inappropriate benefit awards.
entries.examApplication: Distinguish rate/quota from direct control of outcomes.
entries.sourceRole: Case discussed only in assigned casebook Notes; full opinion not reproduced

entries.title: Abrams v. SSA, 703 F.3d 538; Shapiro v. SSA, 800 F.3d 1332 (Fed. Cir.)
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 3, pp. 141–154; user-supplied Chapter 3 continuation (Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: MSPB/courts allowed ALJ discharge for massive case backlogs, ignoring directions or extremely low output.
entries.laymanExplanation: Independent judge must still do the work and manage docket.
entries.legalExplanation: Accountability for neglect of duty does not equal improper merits pressure.
entries.examApplication: Assess proven neglect, fair process, and reason for criticism.
entries.sourceRole: Case discussed only in assigned casebook Notes; full opinion not reproduced

entries.title: ALJ must follow binding agency heads' policy and regulations
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 3, pp. 141–154; user-supplied Chapter 3 continuation (Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: Agency-head review under APA § 557(b) permits agency to make final call on law, policy and even factfinding; presiding officer must apply promulgated controlling policy while may explain disagreement.
entries.laymanExplanation: ALJ can criticize policy, but cannot ignore applicable agency rule in specific case.
entries.legalExplanation: ACUS Rec. 92–7 emphasized heads as policymakers, ALJs as factfinders; legal opinions may explore change but must follow agency precedent absent supersession.
entries.examApplication: Distinguish binding legislative regulation and controlling precedent from nonbinding guidance.
entries.examTrap: An ALJ's personal independence is not freedom to rewrite agency legal policy.

entries.title: ALJs and nonlegislative guidance documents
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 3, pp. 141–154; user-supplied Chapter 3 continuation (Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: Whether ALJs must follow policy statements or interpretive guidance lacking force of law varies; Asmussen upheld superior's direction to examiners to follow hearsay-hearing instructions.
entries.laymanExplanation: Agency's nonbinding bulletin may still direct subordinate hearing staff inside organization, depending on jurisdiction.
entries.legalExplanation: New Hampshire court held examiners employees subject to management over legal/policy interpretations; instructions must not target particular case's outcome.
entries.examApplication: Compare broad policy instructions versus telling a judge how to rule against one licensee.
entries.examTrap: Do not automatically treat guidance as legally binding on courts and public merely because manager tells AJs to follow it.

entries.title: Asmussen v. Commissioner, N.H. Department of Safety, 766 A.2d 678 (2000)
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 3, pp. 141–154; user-supplied Chapter 3 continuation (Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: Court upheld assistant commissioner's general hearing procedures for drivers-license suspension examiners; dismissed examiner resisted instructions.
entries.laymanExplanation: Agency heads can set general hearing policy for AJs.
entries.legalExplanation: Contrasts impermissible interference designed to determine particular case result.
entries.sourceRole: Case discussed only in assigned casebook Notes; full opinion not reproduced

topics.title: § 3.4.2 — ALJ Central Panels and an Independent ALJ Corps (pp. 148–150)
topics.description: State central panels, comparative benefits/drawbacks, Verkuil report's objections to federal central panel.

entries.title: Central panel arrangement
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 3, pp. 141–154; user-supplied Chapter 3 continuation (Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: ALJs are employed by a separate centralized adjudicative agency and assigned to hear cases for subject agencies; agency heads normally retain power to review proposed decisions.
entries.laymanExplanation: A neutral pool of judges loans one to an agency for hearing rather than the agency employing its own judge.
entries.legalExplanation: About half of states and several cities used central panels at book publication; each state has exceptions for particular complex agencies.
entries.examApplication: Distinguish judge employment from who makes final policy.
entries.examTrap: Central panel itself does not necessarily deprive agency heads of final-decision power.

entries.title: Why adopt a central panel?
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 3, pp. 141–154; user-supplied Chapter 3 continuation (Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: Improves appearance of judicial impartiality, may reduce idle local ALJ time by pooling judges, supplies specialized professional adjudication outside enforcement hierarchy.
entries.laymanExplanation: A dental board with five cases/year need not hire a judge full-time; a neutral central pool can supply one.
entries.legalExplanation: Perceived fairness especially important where judge otherwise works for party agency; operational pooling can improve efficiency.
entries.examApplication: Apply to Madison Gaming Board's own AJs and caseload.
entries.examTrap: Actual independence must be weighed against expertise and cost.

entries.title: Central panel limitations
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 3, pp. 141–154; user-supplied Chapter 3 continuation (Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: May create scheduling delays, agency inconvenience, extra payments, weaker subject-matter specialization and institutional turf conflict; Congress never enacted nationwide federal ALJ corps in text.
entries.laymanExplanation: A neutral judge not steeped in the field might take longer and cost more.
entries.legalExplanation: Legislators and agency heads reluctant to surrender control; consult comparative expected caseloads and complex subject matter.
entries.examApplication: Compare cost/effectiveness for routine small hearings versus complex utility regulation.
entries.examTrap: Do not treat neutral appearance as proving lower total costs.

entries.title: Verkuil report: case against federal ALJ Corps
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 3, pp. 141–154; user-supplied Chapter 3 continuation (Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: Authors argue centralized generalist adjudicators might lose specialist expertise, low-cost informality, consistent national policy control and agency coordination.
entries.laymanExplanation: If every benefits judge became like a general federal judge, the system might become expensive and less expert.
entries.legalExplanation: Report contrasts rough judicial tort processing expense with SSA's lower adjudication-budget percentage, as textbook policy comparison not immutable current data.
entries.examApplication: Give both sides fairly in policy essay.

entries.title: Agency heads' control of facts, law, and policy after panel
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 3, pp. 141–154; user-supplied Chapter 3 continuation (Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: In normal state panel model, central ALJ proposed decision remains reviewable by agency heads, who can change legal/policy determinations and often factfinding.
entries.laymanExplanation: Central judge hears evidence; agency's leaders still decide ultimate regulatory policy.
entries.legalExplanation: State exceptions, especially final-order ALJs, separately discussed in § 3.4.3 notes.
entries.examApplication: Identify whether agency head appellate review allowed by this state's act.
entries.examTrap: Do not conflate central panel with independent tribunal issuing nonreviewable orders.

topics.title: § 3.4.3 — External Separation, ALJ Final Orders and the Gaming Board (pp. 150–154)
topics.description: Separate independent adjudicating agencies, Minow letter and ACUS report, states giving final orders to ALJs, Madison gaming hypothetical.

entries.title: External separation of adjudication
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 3, pp. 141–154; user-supplied Chapter 3 continuation (Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: A separate adjudicative agency or tribunal, with no enforcement or rulemaking functions, hears regulatory cases brought by enforcement agency.
entries.laymanExplanation: One agency writes/enforces rules, another acts as judge when cases arise.
entries.legalExplanation: U.S. Tax Court vs IRS, OSHA enforcement vs OSHRC, mine safety and transport safety are source examples. Some countries use broadly centralized administrative tribunal models.
entries.examApplication: Distinguish independent appellate agency from independent initial tribunal; analyze agency policy control.
entries.examTrap: External separation is not simply central-panel assignment while regulator retains all adjudicative powers.

entries.title: Minow letter: an independent administrative court
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 3, pp. 141–154; user-supplied Chapter 3 continuation (Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: Former FCC chair Newton Minow proposed separate judicial body to avoid agency being prosecutor and judge, promote studied written decisions and clearer regulatory policy.
entries.laymanExplanation: People investigating wrongdoing shouldn't simultaneously sit in judgment; an independent court could actually read massive record.
entries.legalExplanation: Source predicts tension between regulator's policy leadership and independent tribunal interpretation; proposal, not controlling law.

entries.title: ACUS 1986 comparative study: independence has institutional costs
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 3, pp. 141–154; user-supplied Chapter 3 continuation (Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: Study found no detectable improvement in adjudicative output attributable to external split but identified coordination costs, interagency lawsuits, competing authority and policy friction.
entries.laymanExplanation: Two agencies can waste time fighting over who controls rules rather than solving disputes.
entries.legalExplanation: Book quotation is historical evidence and part of policy debate, not a constitutional rule.
entries.examApplication: Discuss counterweight to Minow's fairness rationale.

entries.title: Final-order central panel ALJs versus proposed decisions
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 3, pp. 141–154; user-supplied Chapter 3 continuation (Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: Some states give ALJs authority to enter final decisions without general agency-head review; others constrain agency-head ability to change findings, especially those supported by substantial evidence.
entries.laymanExplanation: The state can decide whether a panel judge's result is advisory or the agency's last word.
entries.legalExplanation: Louisiana example particularly restrictive, with no agency appeal; South Carolina, Florida, Texas, North Carolina, Oregon vary in degree and fact standard.
entries.examApplication: In legislative hypotheticals identify precisely who can revise law, fact, policy and what judicial review remains.
entries.examTrap: Avoid treating every state's finality or review standards as identical.

entries.title: Louisiana and Wooley: risks of nonreviewable final ALJ orders
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 3, pp. 141–154; user-supplied Chapter 3 continuation (Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: Where regulator cannot seek review of final ALJ order, one mistaken construction may disable enforcement and create precedent beyond agency's control.
entries.laymanExplanation: A single hearing judge might stop an entire regulatory program by misreading its statute, with agency having no court recourse.
entries.legalExplanation: Wooley v State Farm accepted Louisiana bar on commissioner's judicial review of adverse ALJ order; book criticized policy risks.
entries.examApplication: If recommending finality, address agency's ability to appeal pure legal error.
entries.examTrap: No automatic rule says final ALJ power unconstitutional.

entries.title: Wooley v. State Farm Fire & Casualty Insurance Co., 893 So. 2d 746 (La. 2005)
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 3, pp. 141–154; user-supplied Chapter 3 continuation (Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: Louisiana could lawfully preclude Insurance Commissioner from appealing central ALJ's adverse final order.
entries.laymanExplanation: Statute gave administrative judge a very strong final word.
entries.legalExplanation: Discuss state policy choice and constitutional review constraints.
entries.sourceRole: Case discussed only in assigned casebook Notes; full opinion not reproduced

entries.title: States limit agency-head ability to reverse ALJ facts
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 3, pp. 141–154; user-supplied Chapter 3 continuation (Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: Some jurisdictions bind agency heads to ALJ facts unless substantial evidence or special contrary standard; North Carolina example gives court de novo fact review if heads reverse under 'clearly contrary to preponderance' threshold.
entries.laymanExplanation: Depending on state, agency bosses can change the law but cannot simply swap out credible witness findings.
entries.legalExplanation: Examples: South Carolina/Florida substantial-evidence protection; Texas strong limits; Oregon protects historic more than predictive facts.
entries.examApplication: Distinguish credibility-based historic past facts from future forecasts, legal policy and predictions.
entries.examTrap: Federal APA § 557(b) normally grants broader agency-head review; don't import state limitations.

entries.title: Difference: central panel, final-order ALJ and external tribunal
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 3, pp. 141–154; user-supplied Chapter 3 continuation (Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: Central panel = separate employer of hearing judge; final-order ALJ = judge's ruling becomes final with narrowed/no agency-head review; external tribunal = different agency is adjudicator rather than enforcement agency.
entries.laymanExplanation: Three separate reform levers: where judge works, whose decision is final, and which institution adjudicates.
entries.legalExplanation: Any reform can change administrative policy control, competence, fairness, cost and remedies.
entries.examApplication: Use three separate headings when discussing Madison Gaming Board options.
entries.examTrap: Do not answer all proposals solely as generic 'more judicial independence'.

entries.title: Agency interpretive guidance: conflicting state AJs
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 3, pp. 141–154; user-supplied Chapter 3 continuation (Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: If AJs initially held casinos may exclude card counters, and agency heads issue interpretive bulletin taking contrary view, legislators may choose whether AJs must follow agency's legal policy or adjudicate freely.
entries.laymanExplanation: Agency judges can disagree, but who has the last word depends on delegation and panel structure.
entries.legalExplanation: Madison Gaming Board problem distinguishes internal guidance, formal rulemaking, independent tribunal authority and final-order review.
entries.examApplication: Identify whether interpretive guidance has force for outsiders and supervisory force for agency AJs.
entries.examTrap: A bulletin isn't automatically a binding legislative rule merely because it changes how AJs decide.

problems.title: Type A, B and C classification
problems.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 3, pp. 141–154; user-supplied Chapter 3 continuation (Nov. 24, 2026) (p. 141–143)
problems.prompt: Compare formal APA hearing with ALJ, statutory immigration hearing before AJ outside § 554(a), and administrative benefits decision without evidentiary hearing. Which procedural rights attach from statute versus recommended ACUS best practices?

problems.title: Appointment and removal constitutional challenges
problems.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 3, pp. 141–154; user-supplied Chapter 3 continuation (Nov. 24, 2026) (p. 145–146)
problems.prompt: Differentiate appointment of ALJ by SEC staff under Lucia; lower-court double-for-cause tenure issues; Supreme Court decision in Jarkesy on Seventh Amendment. Avoid treating distinct issues as one holding.

problems.title: ALJ performance and independence
problems.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 3, pp. 141–154; user-supplied Chapter 3 continuation (Nov. 24, 2026) (p. 144–147)
problems.prompt: When could a 500–700 yearly cases goal or removal for massive backlog violate/avoid independence? Contrast AALJ v Colvin, Abrams, Shapiro and never-enacted ACUS performance system.

problems.title: ALJ guidance and headquarters policy
problems.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 3, pp. 141–154; user-supplied Chapter 3 continuation (Nov. 24, 2026) (p. 147–148)
problems.prompt: May adjudicator disregard agency heads' interpretive bulletins, binding regulations, nonlegislative guidance, or instructions to help prosecution? Contrast Asmussen and APA decisional independence.

problems.title: Central panel legislative proposal
problems.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 3, pp. 141–154; user-supplied Chapter 3 continuation (Nov. 24, 2026) (p. 148–150)
problems.prompt: Would a central panel improve the Madison Gaming Board's perceived fairness and caseload efficiency, or lose specialized gaming expertise and policy coordination?

problems.title: Federal corps institutional tradeoff
problems.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 3, pp. 141–154; user-supplied Chapter 3 continuation (Nov. 24, 2026) (p. 149–150)
problems.prompt: Compare pro-central arguments of independence/efficiency with Verkuil report's concerns about expertise, cost, and regulatory policy uniformity.

problems.title: Madison Gaming Board / Card Counting — major textbook problem
problems.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 3, pp. 141–154; user-supplied Chapter 3 continuation (Nov. 24, 2026) (p. 153–154)
problems.prompt: Madison Gaming Board regulates casino licenses and penalties; AJs initially held casinos could exclude card counters. Agency heads issued interpretive bulletin banning exclusion, leading AJs to fine casinos. Industry seeks four separate reforms: (i) adopt central panels; (ii) prohibit judges' reliance on guidance from heads/staff; (iii) make judge decisions final subject to court but not heads; (iv) transfer adjudication to independent Gaming Tribunal. Advise Judiciary Committee whether to adopt each, comparing independence, fairness, expertise, policy uniformity, cost and appealability, WITHOUT solving.

problems.title: ALJ final fact findings across states
problems.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 3, pp. 141–154; user-supplied Chapter 3 continuation (Nov. 24, 2026) (p. 152–153)
problems.prompt: Compare Louisiana, South Carolina, Florida, Texas, North Carolina and Oregon treatment of ALJ final decisions, reversal of historic versus predictive facts and availability of agency judicial review.

problems.title: Independent tribunal and regulator conflict
problems.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 3, pp. 141–154; user-supplied Chapter 3 continuation (Nov. 24, 2026) (p. 151–152)
problems.prompt: What practical benefits and downsides result if the FTC/FCC-like regulator writes rules and prosecutes cases but independent tribunal resolves law, facts and policy disputes?

problems.title: Who sets policy: agency head or adjudicator?
problems.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 3, pp. 141–154; user-supplied Chapter 3 continuation (Nov. 24, 2026) (p. 153–154)
problems.prompt: If gaming AJs follow agency heads' interpretive bulletin inconsistent with prior AJ decisions, when is it proper guidance and when improper decisional pressure? Compare force of law and agency supervision.
